meaning: Reconstruction node for the Akkadian deity Ea (Sumerian Enki): the macron marks a discussable vowel length, not a canonical spelling.

phonemes.desc: Long or tense [eː] — the macron marks a reconstructed vowel length that Assyriologists debate; the sign 𒂍 does not itself encode length.
Open central [a] — the second element of the divine name, written with the sign 𒀀.

pronunciation.approximation: 'EH-ah' — two level syllables, with the first vowel held slightly longer to signal the open question of length.

pronunciation.note: Ēa is Tier 1: the macron is a diacritic the ASCII form loses. It is a pedagogical mark: a visible question that invites discussion about how the name was pronounced in Akkadian. The standard Assyriological spelling is Ea; the Unicode form Ēa belongs to PuniCodex's phonological reconstruction hub.

domains.title: ĒA — The Phonological Reconstruction Hub
domains.subtitle: Abzu, Crafts, Incantations
domains.lead: The name is written 𒀭𒂍𒀀. Standard Assyriology transliterates it as Ea. But in the phonological grammar of Akkadian, the first vowel's length remains an open question — and it is here, in the space between the written sign and the spoken sound, that this temple operates. This node of PuniCodex is dedicated to the phonological reconstruction and didactic grammar of the ancient Near East. We mark vowel length not because it is certain, but because it is discussable. The macron is a question mark made visible.

mythology.lead: The myths of Ea / Enki are stories of intelligent intervention — and they are also data. Every text that names him, from the Sumerian Enki and the World Order to the Babylonian Enuma Elish, is evidence for how the name was read, pronounced, and transmitted. This temple treats those texts as a phonological corpus: each occurrence is a clue to the vowels, stress, and syllable weight that cuneiform signs leave underspecified.

myths.title: Enki and Ninhursag
myths.text: In the Sumerian myth Enki and Ninhursag (ETCSL 1.1.1), the land of Dilmun is a paradise without sickness or death but also without water. Enki impregnates Ninhursag, and a line of daughters follows — Ninsar, Ninkurra, and finally the young goddess Uttu — until eight plants sprout from Enki's own seed set in the marsh. When Enki eats the plants, Ninhursag curses him with eight ailments, one for each afflicted part of his body, and withdraws; only later, persuaded to return, does she seat him by her vulva and bear from his wounded limbs eight healing goddesses, among them Ninti, 'the lady of the rib'. The Sumerian pun is famous: ti means both 'rib' and 'life', the oldest known wordplay on the human condition. Eight diseases, eight remedies, one body of the god — sickness and cure issued from the same source, and the myth reads like a medical text in reverse: the pharmacopoeia is the god's own anatomy, and the healer is the one he wronged.

myths.title: Enki Warns the Flood's Survivor
myths.text: In the Atrahasis epic and the Sumerian Eridu Genesis, the gods, worn out by the noise of humankind, decree a flood to destroy their creation, and Enki is bound by the assembly's oath of silence. He breaks it anyway — not face to face, but through the reed wall of the pious king's house, so that technically the warning goes to a wall (Atrahasis, Tablet I; Eridu Genesis, where the deity speaks to Ziusudra in a dream). The king builds his boat, rides out the deluge, and offers sacrifice when the waters fall; and here the gods learn the counter-lesson — without humans there is no one to feed them (Atrahasis III). This is the earliest known flood narrative in world literature, centuries before Noah, and its theology is startling: the god who saves mankind is the one who cheated, and heaven's survival, not just man's, is the argument for mercy. Loyalty, in Enki's ethics, outranks protocol.

myths.title: Enki and the World Order
myths.text: In Enki and the World Order (ETCSL 1.1.3), the god decrees the destinies of Sumer. He appoints the herding god, sets the sea in its place, regulates the winds and the rains, causes the Tigris and Euphrates to rise — the hymn pictures him loading the two rivers with water 'like a barge' — and above all distributes the me, the divine powers and offices that make civilization run: kingship, priesthood, the crafts, the arts of the smith and the scribe, even the perverse and the sorrowful. Then he sails to Nippur in his boat to have Enlil confirm the whole arrangement. The poem is a theodicy of culture: every institution has its divine origin in one wise node's dispensation, and the cosmos works because competence, not force, is its first principle. When something in Sumer breaks — a canal, a dynasty, a rite — the myth says what broke is a line of custody that began in Enki's distribution.

myths.title: Ea and Apsu in the Enuma Elish
myths.text: In the Babylonian Enuma Elish, the genealogy runs Apsu and Tiamat → Lahmu and Lahamu → Anshar and Kishar → Anu → Ea, son of Anu (Tablet I). When Apsu, the freshwater primal father, plots to destroy the noisy younger gods, it is Ea who acts: he casts his spell, subdues Apsu, slays him, and establishes his own dwelling upon the conquered waters — the house called E-abzu, 'the temple of the Abzu' — founding a line of wise sovereignty that his son Marduk will complete by defeating Tiamat. The pattern — the older water-power supplanted by a wiser one, on the way to a storm-god's triumph — parallels the Hittite Kumarbi cycle and the Greek Ouranos–Kronos sequence. Note the geography of the act: the son of heaven builds his house on the slain father's body. Knowledge, in the Babylonian cosmos, stands on the deep it replaced — the temple of wisdom is literally founded on the waters of the first father.

lore.syncretism: Ea is the Akkadian pronunciation and reinterpretation of the Sumerian Enki. The shift from EN.KI to E-a is not only theological; it is phonological — a new language pronouncing an old name with new vowels. Greek writers later identified him with Poseidôn because of his aquatic domain, though Ea's freshwater wisdom is quite unlike Poseidon's saltwater tempests. In Hellenistic and Gnostic currents, Ea/Enki was linked with Oannes, the fish-tailed culture-bringer described by Berossus. His iconography — water flowing from the shoulders — influenced later depictions of river gods. Each syncretism is a data point in the long history of how the name was heard.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ea survives most visibly as a method: the deity who knows secrets and uses them to save rather than destroy. The flood story, transmitted through Atrahasis and the Epic of Gilgamesh, entered the biblical Noah narrative. The goat-fish became the constellation Capricorn. In modern scholarship, Ea has become a test case for how cuneiform signs map onto spoken sound. The macron on Ēa is our contribution to that conversation — a way of marking uncertainty honestly while keeping the question in view. The name still means: the intelligence that moves in deep water.
lore.extendedMeditation:
This temple does not claim that Ēa is the canonical spelling of the god's name. Standard Assyriology writes Ea, and we honor that convention. What we claim is something different: that the space between the cuneiform sign and the modern pronunciation is worth studying, and that Unicode can be used to make that study visible.

The macron on the first vowel is a pedagogical tool. It says, 'The length of this vowel is discussable.' It turns a silent scholarly debate into a public invitation: learn the grammar, read the tablets, listen to the reconstructions, and decide for yourself. In an era of misinformation, there is radical honesty in marking what we do not know. Ea becomes not a claim, but a question — and questions, like fresh water, are what sustain civilization.

lore.archaeology: The E-abzu temple of Enki at Eridu, excavated by Iraqi and British teams across the twentieth century, lies at the edge of the ancient marshland. Its sequence of shrines, bitumen-lined platforms, and fish-offering deposits marks one of Mesopotamia's longest continuous cults. Babylonian cylinder seals depict Enki/Ea with water streams or in the goat-fish (suhurmašu) form; temple libraries at Nineveh and Babylon preserve the Adapa myth and incantations invoking his wisdom.
